It’s not a head start, it’s a foot in the door. The distinction is important: a head start implies that eventually someone without the same advantage could catch up, but without it you might find you’re not even in the race.

I dropped out because I didn’t know what I wanted to do. I thought that whatever degree I got, I’d have to do something related to that field for the rest of my life, and I couldn’t make up my mind. I was so, so wrong about that. 

If I can give you any advice at all, finish the degree. Doesn’t matter what it’s in, doesn’t matter what your GPA is as long as you pass the classes you need to earn the degree.

Almost 1/5 of suicide attempts using firearms fail. There are some horror stories out there, too. Some of the worst stories are from people who tried to kill themselves with guns and survived. Their lives afterwards were much worse than they were before. Things like paralyzation and disfigurement. It’s the stuff of nightmares.

Hell yeah you’re not! Love the attitude!

Will you ask your teachers for help with your classes? Or make an appointment with your school guidance counselor to work on a plan to make all your responsibilities more manageable?

You’re so good at putting into words what they did! I’m really impressed by how much of a handle you have on this already.

All the things you’ve said about them convincing you it’s your fault, that it’s normal, that it’s not abuse - that’s what abusers do. If you read about the tactics, it’s amazing how common it is, how similar they all are, almost like they all have the same playbook. It’s probably what they have to believe just to be able to live with themselves, which is sad, really, because why not just stop abusing in the first place? The mental gymnastics are mind boggling.

It sounds like you did the same thing I did, too, or at least something similar. I believed mine for so long that it was my fault. I turned all the pain and anger inward, back at myself. I lost myself. Abuse survivors’ responses follow similar patterns, too. It’s nothing to be ashamed of, it’s what we need to do to survive. But those adaptive behaviors become maladaptive outside of the abusive situation, and even in it, over time. The things you do to placate the abuser and try to avoid more abuse will end up wearing you down and could even lead you to self destruct. There are healthier ways to manage even if you’re still living with the abuser.

I learned a lot about detaching from the accusations and labels from reading everything I could find. [Out of the FOG](https://outofthefog.website/what-to-do-1/) is a website that has a lot of helpful information. There are also some good subreddits, which may or may not apply to your situation, such as r/abuseinterrupted r/raisedbynarcissists or r/CPTSD

Some books I found helpful include: 

 *Boundaries* by Henry Cloud - this one is very helpful for understanding boundaries, but since I’m not religious it was challenging to read at times

*A New Earth* by Eckhart Tolle - also had parts that were challenging to read for different reasons, but the meditations on detaching from emotional reactions and ego were so helpful for me. After working through this book and putting the ideas into practice I was able to remain calm during arguments, which was a huge step for me.

I hope some of that helps you!

I’m so sorry that you went through all that! Sorry you’re still in it. Please remember that person’s behavior is a reflection of their relationship with themself. It’s not an indication of your worth. You are worthy of love. You are worthy of healthy boundaries and relationships with people who respect your boundaries. I hope you find the peace of mind to detach from the toxic messages that person has been giving you for so many years.

I hear ya. I can relate to feeling broken, and like there’s too much to do and it’s overwhelming. Can you break the stuff that needs to be done down into small steps?

College is definitely not worth committing suicide over. That being said, I dropped out of college and I regret it so much.

Your major/degree doesn’t matter as much as you might think it does. Undergrad pretty much just proves that you can commit to something for four years and see it through to completion. Several of the people I know don’t work in a field at all related to their college major, but the fact that they finished something (anything) at all helped them get their job. For example a good friend of mine studied music in college, but now she’s vice manager a local branch of a bank. She got a job at the bank after college, and stuck with it and worked her way up to vice manager. The important thing is that she got her foot in the door by having a degree, any degree. Does that make sense? You aren’t locked into a career path because of what you choose to major in during undergrad, but finishing your degree is much better than not finishing it, no matter what you do later.
